## Senior Walk In Bathtubs
URL: https://seniorwalkinbathtubs.com/

Aging Safely Baths helps older adults and their families choose the right **senior walk in bathtubs**: walk-in tubs for seniors with a low step-in door, a chair-height seat and sturdy grab bars, designed for elderly bathers who want to keep bathing on their own terms. We carry soaking, hydrotherapy, bariatric and wheelchair-accessible walk-in bathtubs from Ella’s Bubbles and Hydro Dimensions, installed in as little as one day by factory-certified installers or delivered to your door anywhere in the US or Canada.

Guides for planning a safer bathroom Frequently asked questions Why so many families are replacing the tub first Ask anyone who has helped an aging parent at home, and you will hear the same story. The kitchen is fine. The stairs are manageable with a railing. But the bathtub becomes the one place where everyone holds their breath. That worry is backed by real numbers. When the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention studied bathroom injuries treated in U.S. emergency rooms, it found that injury rates climb sharply with age. Adults 85 and older were injured in the bathroom at a rate of 515 per 100,000 people, nearly nine times the rate of adults in their late teens and early twenties. More than two out of three of those injuries happened in or around the tub or shower, and about 81% were caused by falls. Bathroom injuries treated in U.S. emergency departments, rate per 100,000 people by age (2008) Ages 15–24 58.8 25–34 73.1 35–44 76.0 45–54 70.5 55–64 84.8 65–74 112.1 75–84 241.0 85 and older 515.3 Source: CDC, MMWR 60(22), “Nonfatal Bathroom Injuries Among Persons Aged ≥15 Years — United States, 2008” (2011) , Table 1. Show the numbers Age group Injuries per 100,000 Ages 15–24 58.8 25–34 73.1 35–44 76.0 45–54 70.5 55–64 84.8 65–74 112.1 75–84 241.0 85 and older 515.3 The problem is not bathing itself. It is the climb. A standard tub asks you to lift one leg over a wall that can be well over a foot tall, balance on a wet surface, then lower your whole body down to the floor of the tub. Getting out is harder. You have to push up from the bottom of a slippery basin, often with nothing solid to hold. That is exactly the motion that becomes risky as strength, balance and flexibility change. A senior walk in bathtub takes that climb away. You open a door, step over a low threshold, sit down on a seat at roughly the height of a kitchen chair, close the door and let the water rise around you. When you are done, the water drains, you open the door and you stand up from a seat, not from the floor. For a lot of people, that one change is the difference between bathing on their own and needing help. Standard tub Walk-in tub Lift a leg over a tall wall Then sit all the way down on the slippery tub floor Watertight door Deep seated soak Chair-height seat Grab bar Low step-in threshold (often 3 to 6 inches) The difference in one picture: with a walk-in tub you step through a door instead of over a wall, and you sit at chair height instead of lowering yourself to the floor. What makes a walk-in tub safer than a regular tub Every walk-in tub for seniors is built around the same idea: remove the hard moves. Here are the features that do the real work, in the order most families should care about them. Low step-in threshold. Instead of stepping over the full tub wall, you step over a short sill. In the Ella’s Bubbles models reviewed by the National Council on Aging, the lowest step-in heights ranged from about 3 to 6 inches. Built-in, chair-height seat. Hydro Dimensions walk-in tubs, for example, come standard with a 17-inch-high seat. Sitting down and standing up from a seat is a motion most people already do dozens of times a day. Grab bars where your hands naturally go. Good tubs place a bar by the door and another near the seat, so you always have something solid to hold during the moments when balance matters most. Textured, slip-resistant floor. The floor of the tub is molded with texture so your feet have grip even when the surface is wet and soapy. Anti-scald protection. A thermostatic or anti-scald valve limits how hot the water can get, which matters for anyone with reduced sensation in the feet or legs. Fast-fill faucet and quick drain. Because you sit in the tub while it fills and drains, faucet flow and drain size decide how long you wait. Dual drains empty the tub noticeably faster than a single standard drain. Handheld shower. A hose-mounted shower lets you rinse your hair and body while seated, and lets a caregiver help without leaning over a tub wall. Nice extras such as hydrotherapy jets, heated backrests and chromotherapy lights make a bath more enjoyable, and we are happy to add them. But if you are choosing on a budget, spend first on the fit, the door, the seat, the grab bars and the drain. Those are the parts that keep you safe every single day. A walk-in tub with a low step-in door lets you walk in and sit down instead of climbing over a tub wall. Two ways to get your tub: one-day installation or DIY delivery Most walk-in tub companies only offer one path: an in-home sales visit followed by their own installation crew. We think families deserve a choice, so we offer two. See how ordering, freight and delivery work on our buy a walk-in tub online page. Which walk-in tub fits your body and your bathroom? Walk-in bathtubs for elderly bathers are not one-size-fits-all. The right model depends on three things: how you move, how much room you have, and what you want the bath to do for you. Here is a plain-language map of the main types. Soaking walk-in tubs The simplest, safest deep soak. No jets to maintain. Hydrotherapy tubs Water jets, air jets or both for sore muscles and stiff joints. Bariatric and two-seat Wider seats, wider doors and room for two. Wheelchair transfer tubs Wide outward doors so you slide across, not step in. Small and compact tubs Fits short alcoves, tight bathrooms and shower stalls. Buy online, ship anywhere Drop-shipped to your door in the US or Canada. Tub type Who it suits What to know Soaking walk-in tub Most seniors who want a safe, deep, warm bath The simplest and most affordable option; no jets to maintain Hydrotherapy walk-in tub People with stiff joints, sore muscles or poor circulation who love a massage Water jets, air jets or both; usually needs a dedicated electrical circuit Bariatric or two-seat tub Larger bathers, taller bathers, couples Wider seats and doors; more water to heat Wheelchair-accessible transfer tub Wheelchair users and people who transfer from a chair or walker Wide outward-swinging door so you slide across rather than step in Small or compact walk-in tub Small bathrooms, shower stalls, tight alcoves Shorter length but deep seated soak; check the door swing Lay-down walk-in tub People who want to recline like a regular bath Flat floor and longer length; needs a full-size alcove A few quick rules of thumb help narrow the choice fast: If you use a wheelchair or struggle to step even a few inches, start with a transfer tub that has an outward-swinging door. If the tub will replace a standard 60-inch tub, most models in the 52- to 60-inch range will fit the existing alcove. If you are a larger or taller bather, sit-test the seat width and ask for the interior dimensions, not just the outside size. If aches, arthritis or poor circulation are part of daily life, it is worth pricing a hydrotherapy upgrade. If you have a very small bathroom, look at compact and front-entry models before assuming a tub will not fit. This Old House reports about $4,600 for a standard 60-by-32-inch tub with mid-range materials, with a range of $1,800 to more than $20,000. Retirement Living reports a range of about $4,000 to $22,100. The spread comes from a handful of predictable factors: The tub itself. A basic soaking tub costs less than a hydrotherapy, bariatric or two-seat model. Therapy systems. Air jets, water jets, heated backrests and in-line heaters each add cost. Your plumbing and electrical. Jetted tubs usually need a dedicated circuit, and some homes need a bigger water heater. The condition of the bathroom. Rotten subfloor, old galvanized pipes or a tiled surround that has to be rebuilt all add labor. Who installs it. Professional one-day installation includes labor and removal. DIY delivery shifts that cost to your own installer. We do not publish a price list because two bathrooms that look the same can need very different work. What we do promise is a clear, written quote that separates the tub, the options and the labor, so you can compare it line by line with anyone else. Our walk-in tub cost guide breaks every factor down in detail. A walk-in tub costs less than leaving home Here is the comparison many families find eye-opening. Most older adults want to stay put. AARP’s 2024 Home and Community Preferences Survey found that 75% of adults 50 and older want to remain in their current homes as they age, and 51% said they need a home that supports independent aging. A non-medical caregiver costs a median of $35 an hour, which works out to about $80,080 a year at 44 hours a week. Show the numbers Option Cost Nursing home, private room $129,575 / yr Nursing home, semi-private $114,975 / yr In-home caregiver, 44 hrs/week $80,080 / yr Assisted living community $74,400 / yr Walk-in tub, installed (average, one time) $6,000 once A walk-in tub will not solve every aging-in-place challenge, and it is not a medical treatment. But when the tub is the main thing standing between someone and bathing independently, a one-time bathroom change that costs a fraction of a single year of assisted living is a very practical way to protect both safety and savings. The honest drawbacks, and how we handle them Any company that tells you a walk-in tub has no downsides is selling, not advising. Here is what to plan for. You sit in the tub while it fills and drains Because the door has to be closed before the water rises, you get in first and wait for the fill, then wait again for the drain before opening the door. In a cool bathroom that can feel chilly. The fixes are simple: a fast-fill faucet, dual drains, a heated seat or backrest, and a handheld shower to keep warm water on your shoulders while the tub fills. We size these options to your tub so wait times stay reasonable. You need enough hot water Walk-in tubs are deeper than regular tubs, and many hold more water. If your water heater is small, the last few gallons may run lukewarm. We check your heater size before you buy, and our water heater guide includes a calculator you can use in thirty seconds. The door seal must be installed and cared for correctly A walk-in tub door works like a car door gasket. Installed correctly, it is watertight for years. Installed carelessly, it can drip. That is exactly why we use factory-certified installers and test the seal before we leave, and why the manufacturer warranties we carry cover the door seal. It is a permanent change to the bathroom A walk-in tub replaces your existing tub. If other people in the home prefer to stand and shower, choose a model with a handheld shower and a wall kit, or talk to us about a walk-in tub and shower combination. How our one-day installation works We keep the process short and predictable, because a bathroom that is torn apart for weeks is its own safety hazard. Free consultation. Contact our team by phone, email or form. We ask about the bathroom, who will use the tub and any mobility needs, then confirm whether one-day installation is available at your address. Measurements and recommendation. We confirm the alcove size, doorways, water heater and electrical, then recommend two or three models that fit, with a written quote. Order and delivery. Your tub ships to your home or to our installers. We schedule the install date with you. Installation day. Our factory-certified installers remove the old tub, set and connect the new one, test the door seal, fill, drains and jets, and clean up. Walkthrough. Before we leave, we show you and your family how to use every control, the door latch and the drain, and we answer every question. Paying for a walk-in tub: Medicare, grants and tax credits This is one of the first questions families ask, so here is the straight answer. Original Medicare generally does not cover walk-in tubs , because they are treated as home modifications rather than durable medical equipment. That said, several programs can help, depending on who you are and where you live: Medicare Advantage plans sometimes include supplemental home-safety benefits. Coverage varies by plan, so call your plan and ask specifically about bathroom safety modifications. Medicaid waiver programs , often called Home and Community-Based Services waivers, may pay for home modifications in some states when they are medically necessary. VA benefits. The Home Improvements and Structural Alterations (HISA) grant provides a lifetime benefit of up to $6,800 for service-connected conditions and up to $2,000 for other conditions, applied for through a VA medical center with VA Form 10-0103. U.S. federal taxes. IRS Publication 502 explains when home modifications made for medical reasons can be counted as medical expenses. Canada. The federal Home Accessibility Tax Credit lets eligible Canadians claim up to $20,000 a year in qualifying renovation costs for a senior or a person eligible for the disability tax credit, for a credit of up to $3,000. We do not give tax or legal advice, but we will gladly provide itemized invoices, product specifications and letters describing the safety features so you can submit them to your plan, your VA prosthetics office or your accountant. Our Medicare, grants and tax credits guide walks through each program step by step. Walk-in tubs for Canadian homeowners Most American walk-in tub companies stop at the border. We do not. We drop-ship senior walk-in tubs to homeowners and contractors across Canada, so you can have your own licensed plumber install it. Ask about freight, brokerage and any duty costs when you request a quote, so the full delivered price is clear before you order. Canadian families have strong reasons to plan ahead. The Public Health Agency of Canada reports that between 20% and 30% of seniors fall each year, that falls cause 85% of seniors’ injury-related hospitalizations, and that half of the falls that lead to hospitalization happen at home. The federal Home Accessibility Tax Credit and the medical expense tax credit can both apply to qualifying accessibility renovations, so keep every invoice. For adult children and caregivers Many of our first calls come from a son or daughter, not the person who will use the tub. If that is you, a few tips from thousands of conversations: Start with the conversation, not the catalog. Ask your parent what part of bathing feels hardest: getting in, getting out, standing in the shower, or the fear of being alone if something goes wrong. Their answer tells you which tub to consider. Frame it as independence, not decline. A walk-in tub means they can keep bathing privately, on their own schedule, without asking for help. Most people respond well to that. Include them in the choice. Let them sit in the seat, test the door latch and feel the height of the grab bars if they can. A tub they chose is a tub they will use. Think five years ahead. If a walker or wheelchair is likely, a transfer tub or wider door now avoids a second remodel later. Loop in the whole family early. When siblings share costs, a clear written quote that separates the tub, options and labor makes the conversation easier. Why families choose Aging Safely Baths BBB Accredited with an A+ rating. The National Safety Council reports that 43,020 adults 65 and older died from falls in 2024, and that older-adult fall deaths rose 51% over the past ten years. A walk-in tub is one of the most direct changes you can make to the room where so many of those falls start. Walk-in tub, walk-in shower or roll-in shower? A walk-in tub is not the only way to make bathing safer, and we sell all three options, so we have no reason to push one over another. Here is how they compare in everyday life. Walk-in tub Walk-in shower Roll-in shower How you get in Step over a low threshold and sit Step over a low curb Roll or walk in with no curb How you bathe Seated, immersed in warm water Standing, or seated on a shower seat Seated in a shower wheelchair or on a fold-down seat Best for People who love a soak, sore joints, those who tire standing People who prefer showers and can step a few inches Wheelchair users and people who need caregiver help Waiting Sit while the tub fills and drains None None Water use More Less Less If you love to soak, or standing in a shower wears you out, a walk-in tub is usually the right call. If you never take baths and can manage a small step, a low-curb walk-in shower may be simpler. If a wheelchair is part of daily life now, or likely soon, a roll-in shower or a wheelchair transfer tub deserves a close look. Our guide to walk-in tubs vs. roll-in showers goes deeper, and our wheelchair-accessible shower guide covers ADA dimensions. The best choice matches how bathing actually happens in the home, today and a few years from now. That is the question we start every consultation with. Senior bathroom safety upgrades , in priority order. Wheelchair accessible shower guide with ADA sizes. Frequently asked questions What is a senior walk in bathtub? A senior walk in bathtub is a bathtub with a watertight side door, a low step-in threshold and a built-in seat. You open the door, step in, sit down and close the door before the tub fills. It removes the need to climb over a tall tub wall or lower yourself to the tub floor, which are the moments when many bathroom falls happen. How long does it take to install a walk-in tub? In many homes, our factory-certified installers complete the installation in one day once the tub has arrived. Extra work, such as moving a drain, adding an electrical circuit for jets or repairing a damaged subfloor, can add time, and we tell you about it in writing before the job is scheduled. Is one-day installation available in my area? One-day installation is available in many areas across the United States. Call 1-888-779-2284 or request a quote with your ZIP code and we will confirm availability for your address. If installation is not available, we can drop-ship the tub to you for your own plumber or contractor. Do you ship walk-in tubs to Canada? Yes. We drop-ship walk-in tubs to homes and contractors anywhere in the United States and Canada. Ask about freight, brokerage and any duty costs when you request a quote so the delivered price is clear before you order. How much does a walk-in tub cost? Published national estimates vary. Fixr reports most installed projects cost $3,500 to $10,000, with a $6,000 average, while other publishers report ranges from under $2,000 to more than $20,000 for luxury models. Your price depends on the model, therapy options and the condition of your bathroom. We provide a written, itemized quote. Does Medicare pay for walk-in tubs? Original Medicare generally does not cover walk-in tubs because they are considered home modifications rather than durable medical equipment. Some Medicare Advantage plans, state Medicaid waiver programs, VA grants and tax rules may help with part of the cost, so check with your plan or program directly. Will a walk-in tub fit where my current bathtub is? Usually, yes. Many walk-in tubs are designed to fit a standard 60-inch tub alcove, and compact models are available for smaller spaces. We confirm the length, width, doorway widths and water heater capacity before you order. How long do I wait for the tub to fill and drain? Because you sit in the tub while it fills and drains, wait time depends on your faucet’s flow, your water pressure, the tub size and the drain. Fast-fill faucets and dual drains shorten the wait noticeably, and a heated seat or handheld shower keeps you warm in the meantime. Do walk-in tubs leak? A properly installed walk-in tub door is watertight. Leaks almost always come from installation errors or a neglected door seal. We use factory-certified installers, test the seal before we leave, and carry brands whose warranties cover the door seal. What warranty comes with the tub? Warranty terms depend on the manufacturer and model. Hydro Dimensions provides a lifetime warranty on its walk-in tubs, covering the shell, frame, door seal, motors and parts. Aging Safely Baths adds a 1-year labor warranty on both installed and supply-only orders. We include the written warranty with every quote. ## About Aging Safely Baths
URL: https://seniorwalkinbathtubs.com/about/

Aging Safely Baths helps older adults and their families bathe safely at home. We supply **senior walk in bathtubs**, hydrotherapy tubs, bariatric and wheelchair transfer tubs, and roll-in showers, installed in one day by factory-certified installers in many areas or delivered anywhere in the United States and Canada.

What we do We make bathing safe again for people who have started to dread it. For most of our customers, that means replacing a standard tub with a walk-in tub: a watertight door, a low step-in threshold, a chair-height seat and grab bars where your hands naturally go. For others, it means a roll-in shower, a transfer tub for a wheelchair user, or a compact tub that fits a small bathroom. We sell all of them, so our advice follows the person, not a product quota. You can buy from us two ways. In many areas, our factory-certified installers replace your old tub with a walk-in tub in one day once it arrives. Everywhere else in the United States and Canada, we ship the tub to your door and send your plumber the spec sheets before it arrives. Learn more about one-day installation and buying online . The brands we carry Ella’s Bubbles. We have been an authorized dealer since 2012. Ella’s range runs from compact models to two-seat tubs and wheelchair transfer tubs. Hydro Dimensions. Often our best-value recommendation, with a lifetime warranty on the tub covering the shell, frame, door seal, motors and parts. Meditub. Additional walk-in tub sizes and styles. Bestbath. Including Rane walk-in tubs, transfer baths and roll-in showers. Who runs Aging Safely Baths Aging Safely Baths is run by Zachary Tye Wennstedt . Zach spent years in the plumbing and remodeling business before focusing on accessible bathing. He was a sales manager for multi-million-dollar plumbing companies and managed multi-million-dollar national remodeling companies and their sales teams. He also operates a bath remodeling company. That background shapes how we work: he has seen what goes wrong when bathroom projects are sold with pressure and installed in a hurry, and he built Aging Safely Baths to do the opposite. Zach writes and reviews the guides on this site. He grew up in Boulder, Colorado. You can read more at zacharytyewennstedt.com . How we work Advice before sales. At the same time, AARP’s 2024 survey found that 75% of adults 50 and older want to stay in their current homes. A safe way to bathe is one of the most practical things a family can do to make that possible. Read the full numbers in our bathroom fall statistics guide . ## Bariatric Walk-In Tubs: Extra-Wide, Extra-Long and Two-Seat Models
URL: https://seniorwalkinbathtubs.com/bariatric-walk-in-tubs/

A **bariatric walk-in tub** gives larger and taller bathers the same safety as any walk-in tub, a low step-in door, a built-in seat and grab bars, with the room to actually be comfortable. That means a wider seat, a wider door opening, more space between the seat and the walls, and often a longer interior. This guide explains how to size a bariatric or two-seat walk-in tub correctly, what the extra room costs, and how to make sure it fits your bathroom and your water heater.

On this page Why standard walk-in tubs do not fit everyone What makes a walk-in tub “bariatric” Types of larger walk-in tubs How to size a bariatric walk-in tub correctly What a bariatric walk-in tub costs Hot water: the biggest planning issue with large tubs Floor and structure Getting in and out: design details that help larger bathers Bariatric tub or roll-in shower? Installation and delivery Talking about size with dignity Planning for a couple Larger walk-in tub models at a glance How much a filled tub weighs Measuring the bather: a simple checklist Common mistakes when buying a larger walk-in tub The rest of a bariatric-friendly bathroom When a caregiver helps with bathing Questions to ask before you buy a larger walk-in tub Soaking or jets in a larger tub? Your first bath in a larger tub Why families choose us for bariatric tubs Frequently asked questions Why standard walk-in tubs do not fit everyone Most walk-in tubs are designed around an average-size bather. The seat is comfortable for most people, the door opening is wide enough for most people, and the space between the seat and the front wall leaves room for most people’s knees. But “most people” is not everyone. For a larger bather, a standard walk-in tub can feel cramped in exactly the places that matter for safety. A narrow door opening means turning sideways to enter, which is harder to balance. A narrow seat means sitting on the edge instead of fully supported. A short distance between the seat and the front wall means knees pressed against acrylic and nowhere to shift. For a tall bather, a standard tub may leave the knees out of the water and the shoulders uncovered. A bariatric walk-in tub solves these problems by adding space where the body needs it. Done right, it is not just more comfortable. It is safer, because you enter facing forward, sit fully supported, and stand up with room to move your feet under you. What makes a walk-in tub “bariatric” There is no single legal definition of a bariatric walk-in tub. In practice, manufacturers use the term for models that add some or all of the following: A wider seat. Ella’s Bubbles, for example, offers bariatric models with a 20-inch-wide seat. A wider door opening. Easier to enter facing forward, with or without a walker. More interior width. Room for the hips and arms beside the seat. More depth in front of the seat. Space for knees and feet, so you can stand up with your feet properly under you. Reinforced construction. A frame and floor designed for heavier loads. Longer interior length. Important for tall bathers who want their legs under water. Some bariatric designs also use outward-swinging doors, which leave the whole opening clear as you step in. Types of larger walk-in tubs Type Typical size range Who it suits What to know Wide-seat bariatric tub Often 30 to 33 inches wide Larger bathers who need a wider seat and door Check the seat width and door opening, not just the outer width Extra-long tub 60 inches or more Tall bathers who want legs covered Needs a full-size alcove or larger Two-seat tub 32 by 60 inches up to 36 by 80 inches Couples, or one bather who wants maximum room Many exceed a standard alcove; plan for plumbing and floor space Bariatric transfer tub Varies Larger bathers who transfer from a wheelchair Wide L-shaped outward door for sliding across Two-seat walk-in tubs Ella’s Bubbles is known for pioneering the two-person walk-in tub, and it offers several two-seat models. According to published product details, the Tub4Two measures 32 by 60 inches with seats of about 20 by 22 inches; the Companion is 32 by 60 inches with dual drains; the Escape is 36 by 72 inches with 27-by-29-inch seats and an inward door; and the Big4Two, Ella’s largest companion tub, measures 36 by 80 inches with a centered outward-swinging door, dual drains, and both hydro and air jets plus a foot massage section. Two-seat tubs are also popular with single bathers who simply want all that room to themselves. Extra-long models for tall bathers Tall bathers often find that their knees rise out of the water in a compact tub. Longer models solve that. The National Council on Aging’s review of Ella’s Bubbles notes that its outward-swing line includes a larger tub designed for taller people, including very tall bathers. Other longer options in the Ella range include the 27-by-60-inch Lounger and the 30-by-60-inch Ultimate. Hydro Dimensions specialty series Hydro Dimensions offers 16 walk-in tub models, including a specialty series with bariatric designs and tubs for wheelchair access. Hydro Dimensions tubs are backed by a lifetime warranty covering the shell, frame, door seal, motors and parts, which is especially reassuring on a larger tub that carries more weight. Walk-in tubs come in wider, longer and two-seat sizes for larger and taller bathers. How to size a bariatric walk-in tub correctly The outside dimensions of a tub tell you whether it fits the bathroom. The inside dimensions tell you whether it fits the bather. Here is what to measure and compare. 1. Seat width Measure the bather’s hip width while seated in a firm chair, then add a few inches so they are not wedged in. Compare that to the seat width on the spec sheet. A seat that is too narrow means sitting partly on the edge, which is less stable. 2. Door opening Look for the clear width of the door opening, not the size of the door panel. The bather should be able to walk in facing forward. If they use a walker, the opening and the space in front of the tub both need to accommodate it. 3. Knee and foot room Sit in a chair and measure from the back of the seat to the front of the knees. The tub needs that distance plus room to shift the feet back when standing up. This is the measurement most often overlooked. 4. Seat height A seat at roughly chair height makes sitting and standing easier. Hydro Dimensions tubs, for example, come with a 17-inch-high seat as standard. Taller bathers often prefer a slightly higher seat. 5. Interior length For tall bathers, check the distance from the seat back to the footwell wall so the legs can rest comfortably under water. 6. Weight rating Ask for the manufacturer’s stated weight guidance for the model, and confirm the floor structure under the tub is sound. A filled tub with a bather is heavy, and the floor must support it. What a bariatric walk-in tub costs Larger tubs cost more to build, ship and install. Retirement Living reports bariatric walk-in tubs typically cost $7,000 to $10,000, compared with $2,500 to $5,000 for a standard soaking tub. Fixr notes that two-seat walk-in tubs range from about $6,000 to $20,000 depending on features. Walk-in tub price ranges by type, as published by Retirement Living (upper end of range shown) Standard soaking tub ($2,500–$5,000) up to $5,000 Air bath or hydrotherapy ($5,000–$10,000) up to $10,000 Bariatric ($7,000–$10,000) up to $10,000 Source: Retirement Living (2026) . Show the numbers Tub type Upper end of range Standard soaking tub ($2,500–$5,000) up to $5,000 Air bath or hydrotherapy ($5,000–$10,000) up to $10,000 Bariatric ($7,000–$10,000) up to $10,000 The cost drivers specific to larger tubs are: Size and materials. More acrylic, a larger frame and a bigger door. Freight. Bigger crates cost more to ship. Installation. Larger tubs may need a larger alcove, wall changes or floor reinforcement. Water heating. A bigger tub may need a larger water heater, an in-line heater or a tankless upgrade. Therapy systems. Jets are optional on most bariatric and two-seat tubs, and they add cost. See the full breakdown in our walk-in tub cost guide . Hot water: the biggest planning issue with large tubs The single most common problem with large walk-in tubs is not the tub. It is the water heater. A two-seat or extra-long tub can hold far more water than a standard tub, and most of that fill needs to be hot. Gallons of 120°F hot water needed to fill a tub to 102°F (incoming cold water at 55°F) 40-gallon fill 29 gal 50-gallon fill 36 gal 60-gallon fill 43 gal 70-gallon fill 51 gal 80-gallon fill 58 gal Source: Mixing calculation: hot share = (bath temp − cold temp) ÷ (hot temp − cold temp) = (102 − 55) ÷ (120 − 55) ≈ 72%. 120°F is the setting recommended by the U.S. Department of Energy . Show the numbers Tub fill Hot water needed 40-gallon fill 29 gal 50-gallon fill 36 gal 60-gallon fill 43 gal 70-gallon fill 51 gal 80-gallon fill 58 gal At common settings, roughly 72% of a comfortable bath comes from the water heater. For an 80-gallon fill, that is about 58 gallons of 120°F water, which is more than many household tanks deliver before the temperature starts to drop. Before you choose a large tub, check your heater with the calculator below. Options if it falls short include a larger tank, a tankless water heater sized for the flow, an in-line heater on the tub, or choosing a model with a smaller fill volume. Will your water heater fill a walk-in tub? Pick your numbers. The math runs in your browser; nothing is sent anywhere. Tub fill (gallons) 40 50 60 70 80 100 120 Water heater tank (gallons) 30 40 50 65 75 80 Incoming cold water About 40°F (northern winter) About 50°F About 55°F (typical) About 65°F About 75°F (southern summer) Bath temperature 98°F (warm) 100°F 102°F 104°F (hot tub level) Assumes a 120°F heater setting and that roughly 70% of a tank’s rated capacity comes out hot before the temperature drops. The first-hour rating on your heater’s yellow EnergyGuide label is the more exact number. Floor and structure A filled walk-in tub is heavy, and a large one is heavier still. Water weighs about 8.34 pounds per gallon, so every 10 gallons of water adds more than 80 pounds. Before a large tub is installed, the floor under it should be checked. Our installers inspect the subfloor and framing when the old tub comes out, and any reinforcement needed is quoted before installation day. This is especially important in second-floor bathrooms and manufactured homes. Getting in and out: design details that help larger bathers Beyond size, these details make a real difference: Outward-swinging doors leave the full opening clear as you step in. Grab bars on both sides of the entry , so either hand can steady you. A textured floor that extends to the threshold , so your first step is on grip. A handheld shower on a long hose , so rinsing does not require twisting. Dual drains , so the wait before opening the door is shorter. A heated backrest or seat , for warmth while filling and draining. Want help sizing a bariatric or two-seat tub for your bathroom? Our specialists answer in plain language, with no pressure. For some larger bathers, especially those who use a wheelchair or struggle to lift a foot even a few inches, a roll-in shower may be a better answer than any tub. Roll-in showers have no curb and allow a shower wheelchair or wide shower seat. The 2010 ADA Standards set a minimum roll-in shower size of 30 by 60 inches, and many families choose larger. We supply Bestbath roll-in showers as well as walk-in tubs, so we can recommend either honestly. Read our walk-in tub vs. roll-in shower guide . Installation and delivery Our factory-certified installers install bariatric and two-seat walk-in tubs in many areas, often in one day when the tub fits the existing alcove and the floor is sound. Larger tubs that need a bigger footprint, new plumbing or floor reinforcement can take longer, and we tell you before scheduling. If you prefer to use your own installer, or you live in Canada, we drop-ship the tub to your door with spec sheets, rough-in dimensions and floor-load information for your contractor. Every tub includes the manufacturer’s warranty plus a 1-year labor warranty from Aging Safely Baths. Talking about size with dignity Families sometimes hesitate to ask about bariatric tubs because the conversation feels awkward. It should not be. Choosing a tub with the right seat and door is exactly like choosing a chair or a car that fits. When we help families size a tub, we ask for measurements the same way a tailor would, privately and matter-of-factly. The goal is simple: a bath that is safe, comfortable and dignified every single time. Planning for a couple When two people will share a walk-in tub, the choice gets more interesting. Some couples truly want to bathe together, and a two-seat tub with a centered door lets both enter easily. Others simply share one bathroom and have different needs: one wants a deep soak, the other wants a quick shower. For them, a single large tub with a handheld shower and a surround tall enough for standing showers is often the better fit. Tell us how you both bathe, and we will suggest the layout that works for each of you. Water in the tub Weight of the water alone 50 gallons About 417 pounds 70 gallons About 584 pounds 90 gallons About 751 pounds 120 gallons About 1,001 pounds Most sound residential floors handle a standard tub easily. Larger tubs, older framing, second floors and manufactured homes deserve a closer look before installation. Measuring the bather: a simple checklist You do not need special tools. A tape measure, a firm dining chair and a helper are enough. Seated hip width. Sit in a firm chair and measure across the widest point of the hips and thighs. Add a few inches for comfort. Seat-back to knee. Measure from the chair back to the front of the knees. Seat-back to heel. Measure from the chair back to the heel with feet flat, to check leg room. Shoulder width. Helpful for judging the space between the grab bars and the tub walls. Height. Tall bathers should compare their height with the tub’s interior length. Mobility aids. Note whether a cane, walker or wheelchair is used, and its width. Send these numbers with your quote request and we will match them to models that fit. Common mistakes when buying a larger walk-in tub Buying by outside dimensions only. A 32-inch-wide tub can have a seat no wider than a 30-inch tub. Ask for seat width and door opening. Ignoring the water heater. The tub fits, but the bath runs lukewarm. Forgetting the path in. A two-seat tub may not make the turn into a small bathroom. Choosing a door that swings the wrong way. An outward door needs clear floor space in front of the tub. Skipping grab bars outside the tub. The step from the tub to the bathroom floor needs support too. Overlooking caregiver space. If someone helps with bathing, they need room to stand beside the tub. The rest of a bariatric-friendly bathroom A larger tub works best in a bathroom planned around the same needs. Consider: Wider doorways. Widening a narrow bathroom door makes entering with a walker easier. Grab bars rated for the load, anchored into studs or blocking, not just drywall anchors. A comfort-height or bariatric-rated toilet, with a grab bar beside it. The CDC’s bathroom injury study found that getting on and off the toilet became a larger share of injuries with age. Slip-resistant flooring outside the tub. Good lighting and a night-light. A sturdy bench or chair near the tub for drying off and dressing while seated. When a caregiver helps with bathing For larger adults who need hands-on help, the tub and the room both have to work for two people. An outward-swinging door gives the caregiver room to steady the bather. A handheld shower on a long hose lets the caregiver rinse without lifting or leaning. Grab bars on both sides of the entry give the bather two points of support. And a seat height that matches the bather’s wheelchair or chair makes transfers smoother. If transfers from a wheelchair are part of daily life, look closely at bariatric-capable transfer tubs . Questions to ask before you buy a larger walk-in tub What is the seat width, and how deep is the seat front to back? What is the clear width of the door opening when fully open? How much room is there between the front of the seat and the front wall? What is the seat height from the tub floor and from the bathroom floor? What weight guidance does the manufacturer give for this model? How many gallons does it hold with a bather seated, and can my water heater fill it? Which way does the door swing, and how much floor space does it need? Will it fit through my doorways and hallway? Does the quote include floor inspection and any reinforcement? What does the warranty cover, especially the door seal and any motors? Soaking or jets in a larger tub? A larger tub gives jets more room to work, and many bariatric and two-seat models offer air, water or dual systems. But a larger jetted tub also means a bigger electrical load and more water to heat. If budget or hot water is tight, a large soaking tub with a heated backrest delivers comfort and safety without the extra systems. If you want massage, look at where the jets are placed relative to the wider seat, so they reach your back and legs rather than the space beside you. Our hydrotherapy walk-in tub guide explains the options. Your first bath in a larger tub Take the first bath with someone nearby. Practice opening and latching the door before filling the tub, sit down and stand up once while it is empty, and check that you can reach the grab bars and controls comfortably from the seat. Then fill it, enjoy it, and let it drain completely before opening the door. Why families choose us for bariatric tubs We are not limited to one factory’s sizes. Send the bather’s measurements and a photo of the bathroom, and we will narrow the choices to the tubs that truly fit. Frequently asked questions What is a bariatric walk-in tub? A bariatric walk-in tub is a walk-in tub designed with extra room for larger bathers, typically a wider seat, a wider door opening, more interior width and depth, and reinforced construction. It keeps the safety features of any walk-in tub: a low threshold, built-in seat and grab bars. How much does a bariatric walk-in tub cost? Retirement Living reports bariatric walk-in tubs typically cost $7,000 to $10,000, and Fixr reports two-seat tubs from about $6,000 to $20,000 depending on features. Installation, freight and water heater upgrades can affect the total. How wide is the seat in a bariatric walk-in tub? It varies by model. Ella’s Bubbles offers bariatric models with a 20-inch-wide seat, and some two-seat tubs have seats around 27 by 29 inches. Compare the seat width on the spec sheet with the bather’s seated hip width plus a few inches. Will a bariatric walk-in tub fit in my existing tub space? Some wide-seat models fit a standard 60-inch alcove, while two-seat and extra-long tubs often need more room. We check your alcove, doorways and floor before recommending a model. Is there a weight limit for walk-in tubs? Weight guidance varies by manufacturer and model, so ask for the stated specification for the tub you are considering. The floor under the tub must also be sound, since a filled tub with a bather is very heavy. Do two-person walk-in tubs have two doors? Most two-seat walk-in tubs have one door, often centered so both bathers can enter. Ella’s Big4Two, for example, has a centered outward-swinging door. Will my water heater be big enough for a large walk-in tub? Often not without planning. Roughly 72% of a comfortable bath comes from the water heater at typical settings, so large tubs can outrun a standard tank. Use our calculator, and ask about larger tanks, tankless heaters or in-line heaters. Can a bariatric walk-in tub have jets? Yes. Many bariatric and two-seat walk-in tubs are available with air jets, water jets or dual systems, and some two-seat models include a separate foot massage section. That matters, because Canadian seniors face the same bathroom risks American seniors do. The Public Health Agency of Canada reports that 20% to 30% of seniors fall each year, that falls cause 85% of seniors’ injury-related hospitalizations, and that half of the falls that lead to hospitalization happen at home. What Canadian buyers should know Ask for the full delivered price. Freight to your address, customs brokerage and any duties or taxes should be clear before you order. Hire a licensed local plumber. Walk-in tub installation involves plumbing connections and, for jetted tubs, electrical work. Use licensed trades and follow local codes. Check electrical requirements. Jetted tubs and in-line heaters need a dedicated circuit that meets Canadian electrical code. Keep every invoice. Canada’s federal Home Accessibility Tax Credit lets an eligible senior, or an eligible family member supporting them, claim up to $20,000 in qualifying renovation expenses per year, for a credit of up to $3,000. The Canada Revenue Agency requires documents that identify the vendor, describe the goods or work and show the amount paid. Look at provincial programs too. Some provinces offer their own seniors’ home-safety or accessibility programs, and the medical expense tax credit may also apply to some expenses. See our grants and tax credits guide for more on the Home Accessibility Tax Credit. What your installer will need A walk-in tub is more demanding than a standard tub, so your installer should be comfortable with these tasks. We provide the manufacturer’s documents for each one. Task Why it matters Precise leveling The door gasket must seat evenly along its length to stay watertight Drain alignment The tub’s drain must line up with your existing drain or be relocated Supply connections Fast-fill faucets need adequate supply lines to fill at their rated speed Dedicated GFCI circuit (jetted or heated tubs) Pumps, blowers and heaters need their own protected circuit Wall finishing Extension panels or a wall kit close up the surround cleanly Full fill test Proves the door seal and drain work before the job is called done If your installer has never set a walk-in tub before, that is fine, but they should read the installation manual before the tub arrives and call us with questions. Setting the tub level and testing the door seal with a full fill are the two steps that prevent almost every problem. Every tub includes the manufacturer’s warranty, and Aging Safely Baths adds a 1-year labor warranty on supply-only orders. If your installer has questions during setup, call us. We have been helping families choose walk-in tubs since 2012, and Aging Safely Baths is BBB Accredited with an A+ rating. Understanding freight delivery A walk-in tub is too big and heavy for ordinary parcel carriers, so it travels by freight. If you have never received a freight delivery, here is what to expect. Scheduling. The freight carrier usually calls ahead to set a delivery window. Make sure the phone number on your order is one you answer. Where it is dropped. Many freight deliveries are to the curb or the end of the driveway rather than inside the home. Ask us what service level your quote includes, and plan helpers accordingly. Liftgate trucks. Residential deliveries often use a truck with a liftgate to lower the crate to the ground. Addresses on narrow or steep roads may need special arrangements. Inspection. Open or look through the packaging before the driver leaves. If anything is damaged, write it on the delivery receipt before signing. This is the single most important step for resolving a shipping claim. Moving it inside. Most tubs need two to four adults to carry safely. Measure every doorway, hall and stair on the way to the bathroom before delivery day. A printable checklist for your installer Hand this list to your plumber or contractor before the tub arrives. Read the manufacturer’s installation manual start to finish. Confirm the drain location matches the tub’s drain side and rough-in dimensions. Confirm supply line size and water pressure for the fast-fill faucet. For jetted or heated tubs, install a dedicated GFCI-protected circuit to the manufacturer’s amperage and to local code. Check that the subfloor is solid and level, and repair any water damage. Set the tub and level it precisely in both directions. Connect the drain, overflow, supply lines and any therapy system. Install extension panels or a wall kit and seal all seams. Fill the tub completely and check the door seal along its full length. Drain fully, confirm no standing water, and run every jet, heater and control. Walk the owner through the door latch, faucet, handheld shower, jets and drain. For contractors, remodelers and care facilities If you install accessible bathrooms for a living, we can supply the tubs and showers while you keep the client relationship. Contractors tell us they appreciate: Multiple brands from one supplier , so they can match the right tub to each client. Spec sheets up front , so framing and plumbing can be prepared in advance. Roll-in showers and transfer baths from Bestbath alongside walk-in tubs, for projects where a shower fits better. Delivery to the jobsite , anywhere in the US or Canada. Care homes, group homes and property managers often need several units over time. Tell us about the project and we will help plan a consistent product choice across rooms. Buying from a specialist vs. a big-box store Walk-in tubs are also sold through large home-improvement retailers and general online marketplaces. That can work, but there are real differences. Sizing worksheet: write these down before you call Having these numbers ready makes your consultation fast and your recommendation accurate. Alcove length, measured at the floor, middle and top of the tub area (use the smallest). Alcove width, measured the same way. Height from the floor to the bottom of any window or shelf above the tub. Which side the faucet and drain are on as you face the tub. Width of the bathroom door and any tight hallway or stair turns. Water heater tank size in gallons, and gas or electric. Whether the bathroom has an unused electrical outlet or circuit nearby. The bather’s height, and whether they use a cane, walker or wheelchair. Our measuring guide shows exactly where to put the tape measure. What happens if something arrives damaged Freight damage is uncommon but it happens. If it does, the steps are straightforward: Note the damage on the delivery receipt before signing, even if it looks minor. Take clear photos of the crate and the tub from several angles. Call us the same day so we can start the claim with the carrier and manufacturer. Do not install a damaged tub. Installation can make a claim much harder. Ask about return and damage terms before you order so you know exactly how your purchase is protected. Door styles explained for online buyers The door is the heart of a walk-in tub, and it is the first choice to get right when you are buying without a showroom visit. Inward-swinging doors The door swings into the tub. Because it does not need clearance in the bathroom, it suits tight spaces where a toilet or vanity sits close to the tub. The trade-off is that the door takes up some space inside the tub as you enter, and water pressure helps hold it closed during the bath. Outward-swinging doors The door swings out into the bathroom, which leaves the full opening clear to enter. Outward doors are easier for people who use a walker or need a wider path, and they are standard on most wheelchair transfer tubs. You need enough floor space in front of the tub for the door to open fully. L-shaped transfer doors Transfer doors wrap around the corner of the tub and open very wide, so a wheelchair user can pull alongside and slide across onto the seat. Ella’s Transfer60, for example, uses a 36-inch L-shaped outward door with a 22-inch-wide seat. Front-entry doors A few compact models place the door on the short end of the tub, which can solve very narrow bathrooms. Ella’s Front Entry, at 32 by 40 inches, is one example. Will the tub fit through my house? This is the question that causes the most trouble for online buyers, so measure before you order. Measure the narrowest point on the path: often the bathroom door, a hallway corner or a stair landing. Compare that to the tub’s packaged depth and height, not just its length. A tub can often be tilted on its side through a doorway. Remember door stops and trim reduce the clear opening. Measure between the narrowest points. If the path is tight, removing a door from its hinges often gains an inch or more. Send us your measurements and we will check them against the tub’s shipping dimensions before you order. Spec-sheet terms in plain English Product listings use terms that are not always obvious. Here is what they mean. Threshold or step-in height: how high you lift your foot to enter. Lower is easier. Seat height: how high the seat is from the tub floor. Chair height makes sitting and standing easier. Seat width: the usable width of the seat. Bariatric bathers need more. Water depth: how deep the water gets when you are seated. Deeper means a fuller soak. Gallon capacity: how much water the tub holds. Check this against your water heater. Fast-fill faucet: a high-flow faucet that shortens the fill time. Dual drain: two drains, or a larger drain system, to shorten the wait before you can open the door. Inline heater: keeps jet-circulated water warm during the bath. Anti-scald or thermostatic valve: limits maximum water temperature. Buying a walk-in tub for a parent who lives far away Many online orders come from adult children coordinating a tub for a parent in another state or province. A few things make long-distance projects go smoothly: Get the measurements from someone on site. A neighbor, a local relative or the plumber who will install the tub can send photos and numbers. Photos of the tub, the faucet wall, the bathroom door and the water heater label answer most of our questions. Line up the installer first. Ask a local licensed plumber whether they will install a walk-in tub, and share our spec sheets with them before you order. Choose a delivery day when someone can be there. Freight carriers need a person to sign and inspect the delivery. Plan the walkthrough. Ask the installer to show your parent how to use the door, faucet and drain, or join by video call so you can help later. Keep the paperwork together. Invoices, the warranty and the manual should live in one folder at your parent’s home and one copy with you. We are glad to speak with both you and your parent, together or separately, so everyone is comfortable with the choice. Ready to order? Call 1-888-779-2284, get in touch with our team , or send the quote form with your ZIP or postal code and a few details about the bathroom. A specialist will call you back, confirm the right model and size, and send a written quote with freight to your door. If you later decide you would rather have our factory-certified installers handle everything, and your address is in one of our installation areas, we can switch the order to one-day installation. Frequently asked questions Can I buy a walk-in tub online and have it shipped to my house? Yes. We drop-ship walk-in tubs to homes and jobsites anywhere in the United States and Canada. We provide spec sheets and rough-in dimensions so your installer can prepare before the tub arrives. Do you ship walk-in tubs to Canada? Yes. We ship to homeowners and contractors across Canada. Ask for freight, brokerage and any duty costs when you request a quote so the full delivered price is clear. Can I install a walk-in tub myself? A handy homeowner can do some of the work, but walk-in tub installation involves plumbing, precise leveling for a watertight door seal and often electrical work for jets or heaters. We recommend a licensed plumber and electrician, especially for jetted tubs. What does my installer need from you? The spec sheet, rough-in dimensions for the drain and supply lines, electrical requirements for any jets or heaters, and the installation manual. We send these before the tub ships. Is there a warranty if I install it myself? The manufacturer’s warranty applies, and many manufacturers require proper installation to keep it valid. Aging Safely Baths also provides a 1-year labor warranty on supply-only orders. Ask us for the written terms with your quote. Can contractors and care facilities order through you? Yes. Contractors, remodelers, care homes, group homes and property managers order walk-in tubs and roll-in showers from us for their projects. How is a walk-in tub delivered? Walk-in tubs ship by freight because of their size and weight. Plan to have helpers available to move the tub inside, and inspect it before signing the delivery receipt. Can I claim a tax credit on a walk-in tub in Canada? Canada’s Home Accessibility Tax Credit allows eligible individuals to claim up to $20,000 of qualifying renovation expenses per year for a senior or a person eligible for the disability tax credit, for a credit of up to $3,000. Walk-in bathtubs are commonly listed as eligible. Confirm your situation with the CRA or a tax professional. Walk-in tub basics before you call If you are new to walk-in tubs, here is a five-minute primer so the conversation starts from the same page. A walk-in tub is a bathtub with a watertight door in the side, a low threshold to step over, and a seat built in at about the height of a chair. You open the door, step in, sit down, close the door, and let the tub fill around you. When you finish, the tub drains before you open the door and stand up from the seat. The whole design removes the two hardest moves in a standard tub: climbing over a tall wall and lowering yourself to the floor. Walk-in tubs come in several types: Type Who it suits Soaking tub Most seniors who want a safe, deep, warm bath Hydrotherapy tub People with stiff joints or sore muscles who want massage jets Bariatric or two-seat tub Larger bathers, taller bathers and couples Wheelchair transfer tub Wheelchair users who slide across onto the seat Compact tub Small bathrooms, short alcoves and shower-stall conversions The features that matter most are the door, the threshold height, the seat, the grab bars, the drain speed and anti-scald protection. Jets, heated backrests and lighting are comfort upgrades. The questions we answer every day Some questions come up on almost every call. Here are the short answers, so you know what to expect. “How long do I sit there while it fills?” It depends on your faucet flow, water pressure and the tub size. Fast-fill faucets help. Most people run the handheld shower on their shoulders while the tub fills so they stay warm. “Will my water heater keep up?” Often, but not always. Walk-in tubs are deep. We check your heater size before recommending a tub, and our water heater guide has a calculator you can use yourself. “Do walk-in tub doors leak?” Not when they are installed level and the gasket is kept clean. Leaks nearly always come from installation errors, which is why we use factory-certified installers and test the seal with a full fill. “What does it cost?” Published national figures put most installed walk-in tubs between $3,500 and $10,000, with a $6,000 average, according to Fixr. Your quote depends on the model and your bathroom. See our cost guide . “Does Medicare pay?” Original Medicare generally does not. Some Medicare Advantage plans, Medicaid waivers, VA grants and tax rules may help. See our funding guide . “How long does installation take?” In many homes, one day once the tub arrives. See our installation guide . Why the bathroom is where families start When families call us, it is often because the bathroom has become the most worrying room in the house. The data supports that instinct. In the CDC’s study of bathroom injuries treated in U.S. emergency departments, the most common activities at the time of injury were bathing or showering, slipping, using the toilet and getting out of the tub or shower. What people were doing when a bathroom injury happened (share of injuries, all adults 15+) Bathing or showering 27.5% Slipped 17.3% Using the toilet 14.1% Getting out of tub or shower 9.8% Loss of consciousness 5.5% Getting into tub or shower 2.2% Transferring from wheelchair or walker 1.5% Not specified 16.7% Source: CDC, MMWR 60(22), “Nonfatal Bathroom Injuries Among Persons Aged ≥15 Years — United States, 2008” (2011) , Table 2. Show the numbers Precipitating event Share of injuries Bathing or showering 27.5% Slipped 17.3% Using the toilet 14.1% Getting out of tub or shower 9.8% Loss of consciousness 5.5% Getting into tub or shower 2.2% Transferring from wheelchair or walker 1.5% Not specified 16.7% A walk-in tub directly addresses bathing and getting out of the tub. Grab bars, a comfort-height toilet and good lighting address much of the rest. We can talk through all of it on the same call. A note for family caregivers If you are the person who helps a parent or spouse bathe, you are carrying a lot. Bathing assistance is physically demanding and emotionally delicate, and many caregivers tell us it is the part of the day they dread most. When you call, tell us about your role too: whether you help with every bath, how much lifting is involved, and what worries you most. A tub with an outward-swinging door, grab bars on both sides and a handheld shower on a long hose can make bath time easier and safer for both of you. Sometimes the best recommendation is the one that protects the caregiver’s back as well as the bather’s balance. After the sale: service and warranty support Contacting us does not stop after installation or delivery. If you ever notice a drip at the door, a jet that will not start, or a drain that seems slow, call the same number. We will help you sort out whether it is a simple adjustment, a warranty matter for the manufacturer, or something covered by our 1-year labor warranty. Keep your invoice, warranty papers and the tub’s model and serial number together so we can help quickly. How to vet any walk-in tub company Whether you choose us or someone else, these questions separate trustworthy dealers from high-pressure ones. Do they carry more than one brand? A single-brand company can only recommend its own tubs, whether they fit you or not. Do they give written, itemized quotes? One lump sum makes comparison impossible. Who installs the tub? Ask whether installers are trained or certified by the manufacturer. What is the warranty on the tub, and on labor? Get both in writing. Do they explain the downsides? Fill and drain time, hot water needs and door seal care should come up without you asking. Do they pressure you to decide today? A fair price does not expire at the end of a sales visit. What do independent sources say? Check their Better Business Bureau profile and reviews. Will they sell you a tub without installation? Flexibility is a sign the company is focused on your needs rather than its schedule. Talking with a parent about a walk-in tub Adult children often tell us the hardest part is not choosing a tub. It is starting the conversation. A few approaches help. Start with their goals. “You’ve said you want to stay in this house. What would make that easier?” opens a better conversation than “You need a walk-in tub.” Ask what feels hard. Many parents will admit that getting out of the tub is difficult, even if they would not bring it up themselves. Talk about independence. A walk-in tub means bathing privately, on their own schedule, without asking for help. Offer choices, not decisions. Let them choose between two or three tubs, colors or features. Bring in a neutral voice. A doctor, therapist or a specialist like us can explain options without it feeling like a family argument. Be patient. Some people need a few conversations. That is normal. When you are ready, we are glad to speak with your parent directly, with you on the line or not, whichever they prefer. From first call to first bath Most families are surprised by how simple the process is. A typical path looks like this: you call or send the form; we talk through needs and the bathroom; we confirm measurements, often from photos; you receive a written quote; you place the order when ready; the tub is delivered or installed, usually in one day once it arrives; and you take your first safe, comfortable bath. We give you a realistic delivery estimate with your quote so you can plan around family visits, medical appointments or a hospital discharge. Bathroom safety beyond the tub When you call, it is worth asking about the rest of the bathroom too. The CDC’s bathroom injury research found that the share of injuries linked to getting on and off the toilet grew with age, reaching about 37% among adults 85 and older. A few small changes, often done at the same time as a walk-in tub, cover most of the room: A grab bar beside the toilet, anchored into studs. A comfort-height toilet or raised seat. A grab bar outside the tub for the step onto the bathroom floor. Slip-resistant flooring or rubber-backed mats. Brighter lighting and a motion-activated night-light. Lever-style faucet handles for arthritic hands. Our senior bathroom safety upgrades guide covers each one. We are happy to talk through any of them on the same call, even if you are not ready for a tub yet. Calling for someone who lives far away If your parent lives in another city, state or province, you can still manage the whole project by phone and email. Ask a neighbor, local relative or the plumber who will install the tub to send photos and measurements. We can speak with you and your parent together, send the written quote to everyone involved, and coordinate delivery with whoever will be at the house. For DIY orders, we send the spec sheets directly to the installer so the local work is ready before the tub arrives. If you asked for email, we reply by email instead. If you decide a walk-in tub is not right for you, that is a perfectly good outcome too; we would rather you make the right choice than a fast one. Best times to reach us Most families find the quickest route is simply to call. If lines are busy or you reach us after hours, leave a message with your name, number and ZIP code, or send the form, and a specialist will call you back. For anything urgent, such as a hospital discharge date, say so in your message so we can prioritize it. When bathing already feels unsafe If someone in your home has already fallen in the bathroom, or you are worried they will, here are a few things you can do today while you plan a longer-term solution: Put a rubber-backed, non-slip mat inside and outside the tub. Use a sturdy tub transfer bench or shower chair so bathing can happen seated. Add a handheld shower head, which many people can install without tools. Keep a phone or medical alert device within reach of the bathroom. Leave a night-light on in the bathroom and hallway. Avoid bathing alone in the home until a safer setup is in place, if possible. None of these replaces a walk-in tub or accessible shower, but together they reduce risk while you decide. If you have them, these details help: Tub or shower space: length and width, measured at the floor, middle and top. Faucet and drain side: left or right as you face the tub. Bathroom door width and any tight hallway turns. Water heater: tank size in gallons, gas or electric. Electrical: whether there is an outlet or spare circuit near the bathroom, if you want jets. The bather: height, and whether they use a cane, walker or wheelchair. Photos: the tub from the doorway, the faucet wall and the water heater label. How to compare walk-in tub quotes Whether you get one quote or five, compare them the same way. Compare the same tub type. A soaking tub and a dual-jet tub are not the same product. Check the door direction and threshold. These decide how easy the tub is to use every day. Check the seat width and height. Especially for larger or taller bathers. Check what installation includes. Removal, plumbing, electrical, wall finish, testing and cleanup. Check possible extra costs. Subfloor repair, drain relocation and electrical work should be addressed up front. Compare warranties. What is covered, for how long, and whether labor is included. Check who installs. Factory-certified installers who follow the manufacturer’s specifications protect your warranty. The CRA requires invoices that identify the vendor, describe the goods or work, and show the amount and payment. What changes the number on a quote Two families can choose the same tub and receive different quotes. Here is why, using common situations we see every week. The straightforward swap. An existing 60-inch tub, drain on the correct side, sound floor, a 50-gallon water heater and a soaking tub with no jets. This is the simplest installation, and the quote is mostly the tub and standard labor. The jetted upgrade. The same bathroom, but the family chooses a dual-jet tub with a heated backrest. Now the quote adds the therapy system and a dedicated GFCI circuit. If the electrical panel is full or far away, that line grows. The hidden damage. A tub-for-tub swap where the old tub has leaked for years. When the tub comes out, the subfloor is soft. Our quote lists this possibility in advance with a range, so it is not a surprise, and the repair is done before the new tub goes in. The shower conversion. The home has only a stall shower, and the family wants a compact walk-in tub. Moving the drain, adding a tub filler and finishing the walls adds labor and may add a second day. The large tub and small heater. A two-seat tub in a home with a 40-gallon water heater. Either the tub choice changes, or the quote adds a larger or tankless water heater, or an in-line heater. The long-distance delivery. A DIY order to a rural address or to Canada. The quote shows freight to the door, plus brokerage and duty for Canada, and no installation labor, since the family’s own plumber installs it. Choosing between the models in your quote We usually recommend two or three tubs. Here is how to choose between them. Start with safe entry. The door style and threshold height should match how the bather moves today and in a few years. Then check fit. Seat width, knee room and interior length should suit the bather’s body. Then decide on comfort. Soaking only, air jets, water jets or both, plus heated backrest. Then check the practical side. Water heater capacity, electrical needs and how the tub fits the bathroom. Finally compare warranties. Especially on door seals, motors and heaters. If two options feel equally good, choose the one with the better warranty and the simpler controls. Our installers complete the job and walk you through the tub, or the tub arrives for your installer. Follow-up. We check in after your first few baths to make sure everything is working and comfortable. Pick your numbers. The math runs in your browser; nothing is sent anywhere. Tub fill (gallons) 40 50 60 70 80 100 120 Water heater tank (gallons) 30 40 50 65 75 80 Incoming cold water About 40°F (northern winter) About 50°F About 55°F (typical) About 65°F About 75°F (southern summer) Bath temperature 98°F (warm) 100°F 102°F 104°F (hot tub level) Assumes a 120°F heater setting and that roughly 70% of a tank’s rated capacity comes out hot before the temperature drops. Name and phone number of the person who will answer your questions. Quote mistakes to avoid Comparing a soaking tub quote to a jetted tub quote. Make sure you are comparing the same kind of tub. Ignoring the door direction. A tub that is cheaper but opens the wrong way for your bathroom is not a bargain. Skipping the water heater question. A tub your heater cannot fill will leave you with lukewarm baths or a second purchase. Accepting a lump sum. Ask for the tub, options and labor separately. Not asking about extra work. Subfloor, drain and electrical questions should be answered before you sign. Deciding under pressure. If a price is only good today, walk away and compare. Forgetting the warranty. Compare what is covered and for how long, including labor. Questions to ask about any quote Is this exact model the right size for the bather, not just the bathroom? What will happen if you find water damage when the old tub comes out? Does the price include a new electrical circuit if the tub needs one? Will the tub fit through my doors and hallway? Can my water heater fill this tub with hot water? What does the warranty cover on the door seal, motors and heater? Who do I call if something goes wrong after installation? When can the tub realistically be delivered or installed? Understanding delivery times Walk-in tubs are large, specialized products, and availability changes during the year. Some popular models ship quickly; others are built or configured to order. Your quote will include a realistic delivery estimate for the model you choose. If timing is critical, tell us, and we will point you to models and options that can arrive sooner. It is better to know the true timeline up front than to be promised a date that cannot be met. Canadian quote questions Canadian customers often ask a few extra questions when they request a quote. Is the price in U.S. or Canadian dollars? Your written quote will state the currency clearly. Who handles customs? Ask us how brokerage is handled for your order and what it will cost, so the delivered price is complete. Are duties or taxes charged at the border? Your quote should address this so there are no surprises at delivery. Can I claim the Home Accessibility Tax Credit? Walk-in bathtubs are commonly listed as eligible, and our invoice includes the details the CRA asks for. Confirm your situation with a tax professional. Who installs it? A local licensed plumber, and an electrician if the tub has jets or a heater. We send them the spec sheets. What your quote will not include Just as important as what a quote contains is what it leaves out. Our quotes will never include a surprise “processing fee,” a “today only” discount that disappears tomorrow, or a financing pitch you did not ask for. They also will not include products you do not need. If a feature is optional, the quote says so, and you can remove it.
